The postseason begins on September 29, giving teams one day of rest between the end of the regular season and the start of the race. Playoff teams must plan their rotations early have the right pitchers rested and ready for the opening series and the Boston Red Sox have seemingly made their call.
The Red Sox's rotation for their upcoming matchup with the Cleveland Guardians, their second-to-last series of the year, is Payton Tolle in game one, Sonny Gray in game two and Ranger Suarez in game three. That leaves Patrick Sandoval, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello (or a bullpen game) for the final series against the Chicago Cubs, not necessarily in that order.
Tolle has earned the series-opening start against the New York Yankees. He's posted a 2.36 ERA and 0.88 WHIP with 56 strikeouts over his last seven starts. He's stayed hot despite having 143 innings on his arm this year, and he's gotten even better as the year has gone on.
Tolle has had previous success against the Yankees, including two stellar outings this year. He faced the Yankees in his first big league appearance this year and allowed just one run on three hits with 11 strikeouts and a walk over six innings. Tolle next faced New York on June 26 (one of the games in the four-game sweep that started Boston's historic summer winning streak) and he pitched seven, one-hit innings with seven strikeouts.
Red Sox-Guardians series likely previews Boston's Wild Card rotation with Payton Tolle starting Game 1
Starting Tolle first could set up a battle between two young lefties and Cy Young Award contenders (though it isn't much of a contest) if the Yankees plan to open the series with their ace Cam Schlittler. This might not be the case, though, as New York seems to be setting Gerrit Cole up for the Game 1 start. The Red Sox don't fare as well against right-handed pitching as they do against lefties, with a .712 team OPS against them, and taking Boston off its game will be a high priority for its rival.
Whether the Red Sox win or lose Game 1, Game 2 means everything. With a series loss or a sweep on the line, Boston's ace Gray should take the mound. The 36-year-old Gray has surprised fans everywhere by posting one of the best seasons of his career with the Red Sox and his consistency is unmatched.
Gray has clocked a 2.82 ERA, 1.16 WHIP, 146 strikeouts and 45 walks over 163 innings. Like the Red Sox, the Yankees also don't perform especially well against righty pitching, with a .713 OPS as a club. With a sweep on the line or to stay alive, the veteran Gray is the guy to trust.
In a win-or-go-home Game 3, Suarez deserves Boston's trust. He's gotten back on his feet over the last few weeks following a shaky spell (5.70 ERA in August) after a groin injury. Postseason starts are Suarez's bread and butter — he boasts a 1.48 ERA and 1.06 WHIP over 42.2 frames across seven playoff series — and he's the best choice to keep the Red Sox alive when they're on the brink of elimination.
Boston's rotation has been the biggest strength of the team all season. With these three pitchers, in any order, the Red Sox have good chances to get past the Yankees to advance to the Division Series. But setting the energy with Tolle and having the two veterans follow, as Boston has set things up, makes a lot of sense.

The Red Sox tied controversial chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's future to the Boston franchise through 2030 on Tuesday, extending his grip on baseball operations after a season that at one point looks like it would have cost him the job.
The move, announced alongside a three-year contract making interim skipper Chad Tracy the club's 49th manager, arrives five months after a coaching purge and a fan revolt threatened to end Breslow's tenure early.
Born in New Haven and raised in nearby Trumbull, Connecticut, Breslow grew up attending Congregation B'nai Israel in Bridgeport, where he had his bar mitzvah in 1993. His older sister's childhood cancer diagnosis, when Breslow was 12, pointed him toward medicine long before baseball made that detour permanent.
Red Sox Turbulence Under Breslow
Breslow retired as a player following a stint with the Cleveland franchise, then called the Indians, in 2017. He stated a new baseball career in the front office in 2019, when Theo Epstein brought him to the Chicago Cubs as director of strategic initiatives. He rose to assistant general manager and senior vice president of pitching before the Red Sox hired him as chief baseball officer in October 2023, replacing Chaim Bloom.
His tenure produced long-term extensions for core players such as Brayan Bello, Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony — and no shortage of turbulence. The 2025 trade of Rafael Devers to the San Francisco Giants reportedly fractured his standing in the clubhouse, and ESPN's Jeff Passan reported Breslow's circle of trust had narrowed, with one loyalist warning that "turncoats" were plotting against him internally.
Criticism intensified in April 2026, when Breslow fired manager Alex Cora and six coaches following a 10-17 start. A plane towed a banner over Fenway Park demanding his firing, and Boston Globe columnist Dan Shaughnessy branded his player evaluations "horrendous."
Team president Sam Kennedy insisted that June that dismissing Breslow was "not even on the table", even as national voices called it nearly impossible to picture Breslow surviving the year.
The the turnaround happened. From a 32-46 low point, the club reeled off a 15-game win streak from July 3 to July 22 went 38-16 in July and August clinching their second straight postseason berth on Sunday.
"When you reach a certain level of conviction, you have to act," Breslow said of the gambles that defined his season, according to The Boston Globe's Alex Speier.
Kennedy cited that same conviction Tuesday in explaining the new deal.
"Results matter greatly in this business, but so do judgment, character, and the ability to bring out the best in others," Kennedy said in a statement posted by the team — a verdict on Breslow's most scrutinized season yet.
Breslow's Path to Boston Red Sox Top Job
He captained Trumbull High School's baseball and soccer teams before enrolling at Yale, where he led the Ivy League with a 2.56 ERA as a senior and graduated in 2002 with a molecular biophysics and biochemistry degree. He deferred admission to NYU's medical school to chase a professional pitching carer, a gamble that later earned him The Wall Street Journal's "Smartest Man in Baseball" label and a No. 1 spot on The Sporting News' smartest athletes list.
The Milwaukee Brewers drafted him in the 26th round in 2002, and he debuted with the San Diego Padres in 2005. Breslow pitched 12 big league seasons for seven organizations, posting a 3.45 ERA over 576 appearances, with his sharpest stretch coming during with the Red Sox during Boston's 2013 title run, when he posted a 1.81 ERA and didn't allow an earned run in nine of 10 postseason outings. That championship made Breslow one of only four former Red Sox players to later run the club's baseball department.

Ranger Suarez is back to having fun after clinching the playoffs. Despite losing on Sunday, the Boston Red Sox clinched their spot in the postseason due to other teams' losses. The Sox took a team picture on the field at Tropicana Field before heading into the clubhouse for the usual champagne showers and beer.
In the team photo, Suarez clearly sticks out. Standing right in the middle, the lefty starter had bright red shorts pulled up well above his waist, and his celebratory shirt tucked in. He was also the only player in the picture with his goggles already covering his eyes. Suarez was known as a fun celebration guy with the Philadelphia Phillies, and it was something the fans there loved about him; Red Sox Nation was just waiting to see in Boston.
While Suarez is all fun and games with good spirits during a celebration, he does a complete 180 once the playoffs start. He's been one of the best playoff pitchers ever. His 1.48 ERA is the sixth-lowest of all time among pitchers with at least 40 innings pitched in the playoffs.
The 31-year-old has pitched in each of the last four postseasons. In 2023, he allowed just two earned runs in 14 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed four earned runs in 18 2/3 innings. In 2024, he allowed no runs in 4 1/3 innings. In 2025, he allowed one earned run in five innings. In the regular season, the lefty has a career 8.4 K/9; in the playoffs, it's 9.3
Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree should excite fans after last season's playoff rotation
His playoff excellence was part of the reason the Red Sox signed him. While Suarez has been a very solid regular-season pitcher, it was his success in the playoffs that really made him stand out in last season's free-agent pool. After Garrett Crochet, the Red Sox ended up relying on Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. The Sox knew they needed another playoff-tested arm for the postseason and made the splash signing of the lefty to do so.
The Red Sox now head into the 2026 playoffs with a projected Wild Card round rotation that will consist of Suarez, Sonny Gray, and Payton Tolle. While the exact order is yet to be determined, those three arms will instill much more confidence than the three who started the games last year.
Suarez likes to have his fun. He did so in Philly and is doing so again here in Boston. That doesn't mean that opponents should take him lightly. Come playoff time, Suarez turns it on and shuts down the other teams.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

Every Monday, this column will break down the most popular waiver wire and free agent acquisitions from the weekend. I dig into the top adds on the ever-popular Fantrax and in the NFBC Online Championship (OC), a national mid-stakes contest with 240 total leagues of 12 and a six-figure grand prize. Reviewing player adds between the two should provide us with a well-rounded perspective and barometer of the fantasy baseball marketplace.
Week 26 Overview
Hitters
The San Diego Padres took advantage of their four-game series with the Rockies at Coors Field and a home set with the Marlins, scoring 51 runs, 12 more than any other team. Fernando Tatis Jr. (along with Brandon Lowe and Pete Crow-Armstrong) led the way with a week-high four dingers. Last week’s streamers turned out to be dynamite: Jake Cronenworth (.464-8-2-8-2), Dustin Harris (.379-5-0-7-2) and Samad Taylor (.556-6-1-7-1) really stepped up, particularly Taylor for my competitive Main Event squad that gained two category points in batting average last week. Rake Cronenworth was true to his nickname from several years ago. He led all Major League hitters with 13 hits. The Brewers swiped a league-high 12 bags last week: four each for Jackson Chourio and rookie Cooper Pratt. Tampa’s Chandler Simpson led all runners with five swipes, finally catching Washington’s Nasim Nuñez for the MLB lead with 46. Expect Simpson to finish with 50+ and win the stolen base crown.
Pitchers
Of the 29 two-start pitchers excluding Pirates opener Lake Bachar, three earned two wins: Tarik Skubal, Sean Burke and David Peterson. Houston’s Hunter Brown had an outstanding two-step (10 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 5 K – 20 K) and those 20 punchouts led all pitchers for the week. Gavin Williams punched out 16 in 12 innings and is back atop the AL lead in strikeouts with 244. Dylan Cease (239) may not make his final start of the season and Cam Schlittler (234) is unlikely to catch Williams as both have one start remaining. It’s very possible that Williams catches and passes Jacob Misiorowski (247) for the Major League lead. The Miz pitched three innings in his weekend start and might be limited for his final one.
Tampa’s Bryan Baker was the first reliever to reach 40 saves this season. It’s possible that Cade Smith (39), Riley O’Brien (38) and Mason Miller (37) join Baker. The last time there were three closers with 40 or more saves was in 2019: Edwin Díaz (57), Wade Davis (43), and Craig Kimbrel (42). Shout out to folks who drafted O’Brien late, and/or picked up Baker, Louis Varland or Jacob Latz off waivers and didn’t have to worry about the saves category all season.
Week 27 Most Added Players: NFBC Main Event, NFBC OC, and Fantrax
It’s the last hurrah for managers with FAB dollars left, hoping to get the best bang for the buck and for variance to lean their way and tip them into league titles. As is usually the case in the final week, we hope to optimize our pitching rotations and hitters in hitter-friendly ballparks against bad pitching. It was odd seeing Shohei Ohtani available in several leagues, and perhaps fortuitous as he should be activated this week and start a few games. Ohtani was acquired in 26 OCs for an AWB of $17. In Main Events, there were 12 shares available and they went for a reasonable $12 a pop. I scooped up a rare Ohtani share in an OC for $2, winning a tiebreaker over the team in 1st place in that league. Andy Pages will be activated on Tuesday, which should push Tommy Edman back to second base. Pages had been out since August 21, but was producing at an exciting clip before the injury — .272 – 72 R – 21 HR – 80 RBI – 12 SB in 550 PA. Managers who acquired him are hoping that he dusts the cobwebs back off and gets right into the swing of things, with all the marbles on the line.

Pitchers were the most popular targets, specifically two-steppers, as we chase wins and strikeouts, hoping the Ratio Monster doesn’t eat our leads in ERA and WHIP. JR Ritchie and Daniel Lynch IV were the most added starters who we expect two starts from this week. Ritchie’s MLB debut back in April came with great promise, but walks haunted him greatly, which led to trips back to Triple-A to refine his craft and some bulk inning relief work when he returned to Atlanta in July. Ritchie was recently promoted again, and ran into a juggernaut Cubs offense last week, allowing six runs on seven hits in 4.2 innings. The walk rate (13.7%) isn’t pretty, and he has a good opportunity to end his season on a high note with two reasonable matchups — against the Reds at home and the Marlins on the road. Lynch had served the Royals well as their top southpaw out of the bullpen for most of the season. He moved to the rotation in August and slowly worked his pitch counts upward. Lynch has made it to five innings in each of his last three starts. His latest one (at HOU on September 16) went well — 5 IP – 2 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 3 K. More of that please as he faces the White Sox and Guardians at Kauffman Stadium in the final week. If I could only choose one for the week, it would be Ritchie.
Red Sox pitchers Brayan Bello and Garrett Whitlock were popular buys as the likelihood of roto stars shining bright on them this week is high. Bello is coming off a tremendous outing against the AL-leading Rays on Saturday where he posted an 11:0 K:BB with just one run allowed in eight innings. Those 11 punchies tied his career high. Bello had been the worst starter in the game (6.49 ERA, 1.67 WHIP) through June 4, when he was optioned to Triple-A. Since the All-Star break, mostly out of relief and with two starts, the 27-year-old has been shining. Over those 51.1 innings, he is rocking exemplary ratios (2.28 ERA, 1.01 WHIP) and a 17% K-BB% (22.3% K, 5.3% BB). Bello should make a start against the Cubs next Saturday. The Cubs should be settled into a playoff spot by then, so perhaps they give Pete Crow-Armstrong and some of the other regulars that day off. Boston’s closer Aroldis Chapman has been day-to-day with a lat issue, so perhaps the Red sox have him take it easy and provide Whitlock with some save opportunities. Whitlock has a 7-2 record with a 17.5 ERA, 0.88 WHIP and four saves.
Streaming Diamondbacks is a good idea this week, specifically for their three-game set at Coors Field against the Rockies in the early part of the week. Pavin Smith was a coveted target, coming off a four-day stretch where three of his hits were home runs. Don’t expect Smith to start against lefty Kyle Freeland, but he should be in the lineup for the other two contests against righties. Nolan Arenado was available in one of the 60 Main Event leagues and was acquired for just one dollar.
Better late than never for two punchless Padres who have been quite productive and certainly enjoyed their visit to Coors Field in the first half of last week. Dustin Harris ($10 AWB) and Samad Taylor ($5) have been red hot and playing often over the last 10 days. Though he doesn’t have a home run yet, Harris has been quite productive and helpful to early-bird managers: eight runs, 12 runs batted in and three steals, batting .384 with a 166 wRC+ in 40 plate appearances since September 11. He’s also been batting second against right-handed starters. Taylor has at least one hit in nine of his last 10, including a 3-for-3 effort on Sunday, and has driven in seven in his last seven games.

Sutter Health Park is not a fun place to pitch, but the A’s lineup is a watered-down version without Brent Rooker, Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, and Jacob Wilson윌슨. Javier’s first start is in Seattle may not be a picnic with gluten-free granola and Pearl Jam on the Discman.
Milwaukee’s Robert Gasser only draws one start (home vs. STL), but is considered a reliable ratios guy who can score a much-needed win for fantasy managers, as the Brewers will certainly be favorites in that matchup. Gasser earned his fifth win on Saturday, throwing seven scoreless innings against the Orioles. White Sox lefty Anthony Kay has good matchups (at KC on Tuesday and vs. COL on Sunday), though that second start could be pulled away from him. The main problems here is that Kay hasn’t made it to the fifth inning in any of his last five starts. I feel much more comfortable with a single start against the Orioles from Max Scherzer than I do a double (at SEA, at ATH) from wily Yusei Kikuchi. It’s possible that attraction towards Ryan Johnson this weekend relates to dynasty and keeper formats, and not his start in Seattle this week. Johnson has limited run damage over his last nine starts, since August 6, posting a 2.39 ERA, but with an xFIP (5.01) nearly double the mark. Johnson is more of a 4.25-4.50 ERA guy than a sub-3.00 ERA one, as his 90.9% LOB and .229 BABIP portends.
Perhaps a similar mindset applies to folks who scooped up Jack Perkins, who pitched two quality starts on the road against the Rays (6.2 IP – 4 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 8 K) and the Guardians (6 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 0 BB – 4 K), flashing some of his upside and future potential. Perkins has had a difficult season (5.90 ERA, but a 4.16 xFIP, 1.45 WHIP) and will be a tough streamer at home in Sacramento next season, but the strikeouts (25.2%) should always be there.
Andrew Alvarez should have a rotation spot with the Nationals next season. He has been outstanding since the All-Star break, posting a 2.44 ERA (3.30 FIP, 4.02 xFIP) with a 1.10 WHIP and a 22.7% strikeout rate, though he wasn’t able to secure a win in any of those 10 starts. Alvarez won’t be a particularly coveted target in drafts next season, but should have a NFBC ADP somewhere in the 250-325 overall range. He may be a consideration in NL-only keeper leagues with deep benches and five-plus keepers.

Gavin Williams and Jacob Misiorowski finish the season tied for the MLB lead in strikeouts with 255. Williams punches out 11 and Misiorowski, eight.
JR Ritchie steps up for his two starts and has a Jack Perkins Week 26 type week, helping managers win league titles.

One of Cristian Javier or Yusei Kikuchi will remind why streaming pitchers in Sutter Health Park, even if part of a two-step, is a mistake.
Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery hit three home runs each this week and the White Sox score the most runs in Week 27.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

The Boston Red Sox's Wild Card clinching ceremony included the usual champagne showers and dripping-wet interviews. Everyone had their moments between the clubhouse party and the team photo, but the expected star of the celebration did not disappont.
Payton Tolle gave Red Sox fans everything they wanted and more out of their playoff-making party. The towering lefty is usually the most hilarious member of the Red Sox, but his antics were turned up to 11 in the presence of more beer than anyone can drink.
Tolle smashed some beers Stone Cold style, danced like no one was watching and gave an under-the-influence interview fans won't soon forget. The best part is that he would probably do many of the same things sober as a judge.
Tolle has grown in to a Red Sox fan favorite in record time. His off-the-field shenanigans match up to the skill he brings on the mound. After his first season-plus with Boston, it should be doing everything in its power to keep Tolle on the team for as long as possible.
Payton Tolle's Wild Card celebration showed just how badly the Red Sox need to extend him
The Red Sox have adopted an early contract extension strategy with many of its young players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Brayan Bello and Roman Anthony, among others. Alex Speier of The Boston Globe reported on August 18 that Boston hadn't approached Tolle about an extension at the time (subscription required). The Sox have signed so many young players that they could be taking a break, but they should re-start negotiations again for Tolle.
Not only is the 23-year-old an electric personality, he's a force on the mound. The American League's 2026 rookie class is packed to the brim with talent including Kevin McGonigle (the certain winner), Parker Messick and Munetaka Murakami, but Tolle has performed well enough to deserve a mention near the top of this year's list.
Tolle has posted a 3.02 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 166 strikeouts and 38 walks over 143 innings. The rookie has deepened and sharpened his arsenal this season, his extension (a metric Craig Breslow loves) is elite at a staggering seven-foot-four, his 36.5 percent chase rate sits in the 96th percentile and his 28.9 strikeout percentage ranks near the top of the league. Tolle is an imposing presence on the mound with the prime of his career still years away and the Red Sox should hold onto him for as long as possible.
Tolle will most likely get a start during Boston's Wild Card series, possibly in Game 1. The Red Sox clearly trust him in big moments, he's got personality to share and he's already active in the community — he is the ideal candidate for an early contract extension.

The Boston Red Sox are set for a pivotal playoff matchup, likely with the New York Yankees in the first round of the postseason.
It’s been a whirlwind of a season for Boston fans after their horrible start under manager Alex Cora and subsequent hot streak under interim manager Chad Tracy. Part of this hot streak has been the emergence of an elite rotation led by rookies and veterans alike.
Their rotation is so good, in fact, that it’s a real discussion of who will start Game 1 and Game 2 between Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suárez. And it’s a good problem to have!
Rob Bradford of WEEI shared that Tolle has a “good shot” at taking the mound in the first game of the series. If he gets the ball in Game 1 or Game 2, he will make franchise history as the youngest pitcher to start the first or second game of a playoff series since Babe Ruth in the 1918 World Series, per former Red Sox director of baseball communications and media relations JP Long.
Should Boston Red Sox Phenom Payton Tolle Start Game 1 or 2?
The Red Sox drafted Tolle in the second round of the 2024 MLB Draft out of Texas Christian University. Teams quickly saw that Tolle had the tools to succeed, as he sprinted through the minors.
He would soon have an elite year in the minors in his first professional season, making it all the way to the majors in 2025. However, it was rough sledding for Tolle as he sported a 6.06 ERA in 16.1 major league innings.
Going into 2o26, he was a top-20 prospect. From the start of the season, he has not disappointed. In 25 starts during 20026 (143 innings), Tolle has a 3.02 ERA with 166 strikeouts and just 38 walks.
He has the second-lowest ERA among qualified starters on the team, just behind Sonny Gray. While you could definitely make an argument that the veteran Gray should start Game 1, Tolle has been a monster against the Yankees this season.
In his season debut on April 23, Tolle went six innings, allowing just three hits, one walk, one run and striking out 11 batters. On June 26, he would face New York again, going seven innings and allowing just one hit and two walks with seven strikeouts.
Gray has the regular-season production, postseason experience and fuel, being a former Yankees castoff. However, Tolle seems to be at his best when playing against New York and other AL East teams.
Either way, Tolle will likely be making history not seen since the Great Bambino in over a century.
What About Game 3 and Moving Forward?
Suárez should be locked in for a top-3 start, if necessary. In 27 starts, Suárez has a 3.27 ERA in 143.1 innings with 135 strikeouts. The two-time All-Star is also a formidable playoff pitcher, with a minuscule 1.48 ERA in 11 postseason games.
After him, it gets a bit murkier. While you don’t need a full five-man rotation in the playoffs, it’s likely necessary to have a fourth dependable starter.
Rookie Jake Bennett was cruising through his first dozen career starts. However, in his last seven starts, he has a 5.40 ERA. He may be unlikely to shoulder such a burden in his first postseason. It also complicates things that 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet has been out since late April and will likely be a bullpen arm if and when he returns in 2026.
And perhaps the most shocking positive development has been the improvement of Brayan Bello. In his first 10 games, Bello was a disaster. In his last 15, he has been borderline elite with a 2.98 ERA. This was highlighted by an eight-inning performance on Saturday. If needed, Bello could likely be a starter or bulk reliever in the playoffs.
Whatever the case may be, the Boston Red Sox could be a dangerous team in October, with their monster pitching staff at the head of it all.

Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

Boston Red Sox right-hander Kutter Crawford was set to make a rehab start with Triple-A Worcester. But with the game being cancelled due to rain, per the Worcester Telegram-Gazette's Tommy Cassell, the club faces a tough roster decision on the 30-year-old starter.
The cancellation also ends Worcester's season. That means the Red Sox will have to decide if they want to roster Crawford during the final seven games of the regular season, and possibly the postseason.
Crawford is currently on the 60-day injured list after suffering a major setback in his recovery from wrist surgery. After a rehab start in April, he experienced issues in his right elbow and has been shelved since. This appearance would have been his first outing in five months.
Red Sox Face Tough Roster Decision on Kutter Crawford
With nowhere to get a rehab outing, the Red Sox will have to decide the next steps for Kutter Crawford. They certainly had some contingency in place if the game was affected by weather.
The first question the Red Sox have to answer is whether Crawford is an option for the postseason. If not, they will likely just shut him down. Otherwise, they have to clear a 40-man roster spot to activate him from the injured list.
If Boston does roster the 30-year-old, it will likely be in a relief role. The Red Sox will likely go into the Wild Card Series with a three-man rotation of Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, and Payton Tolle. If they advance further, they could turn to either Jake Bennett or Brayan Bello as their fourth starter.
Given the postseason in general, there could be some need for an innings-eater for the bullpen. But Bello and Bennett are further stretched out than Crawford at this point in the season.
If Crawford is done for the year, it will mark the second straight season the right-hander has not thrown a pitch for the Red Sox. That could make him a non-tender candidate in November. But if they do tender him, he won't see much of a raise from his $2.75 million salary for 2026.
It's quite possible that Crawford has thrown his last pitch for the Red Sox.
Red Sox Right Now
The Red Sox aim to clinch a postseason berth in their series finale against the Tampa Bay Rays. They'll send left-hander Patrick Sandoval to the mound.
Boston needs a win or a loss by the Houston Astros to officially clinch. They've already been eliminated from American League East contention, so they would be locked into a Wild Card spot.
The Red Sox have a five-game lead for the AL's second Wild Card spot. So they should lock in their postseason seeding in the next couple of days. That would allow them to set up their rotation for the Wild Card Series. Their likely first opponent in the postseason will be the New York Yankees.

The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

X-rays on Willson Contreras’s hand were negative, but don’t take that to mean everything is sunshine, rainbows, and Swiss cheese. Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
Contreras won’t be on the field for a few days, but he’s still in the clubhouse. That wasn’t the case for Roman Anthony, who was sent to Fort Myers during his rehab, where he worked hard to stay connected to the team. “Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.” (Tara Sullivan, Boston Globe)
But now that he’s back in the big leagues, it’s time for Roman to start producing more consistently. He did some extra hitting work before this series against the Rays began and the team is confident he’s going to really get going. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows,” said Chad Tracy. “He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
Garrett Crochet isn’t with the time right now, but he’s still trying to get back with them. He donned his full uniform yesterday at Polar Park in Worcester and threw 20 pitches, topping out at 92 MPH. The Sox hope he can throw to live hitters at Fenway later this week. Tanner Houck, meanwhile, threw 3.1 innings for the WooSox in his final rehab appearance. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
A healthy Crochet and Houck could make for a formidable bridge to the back of the bullpen. And after yesterday’s outstanding start, Brayan Bello has also shown that he’s ready to be a part of the postseason action. “For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
If Crochet and Houck do make it back to the roster, hopefully their transition will be as seamless as Trevor Story’s has been. “The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be,” he said, “and it’s starting to show.” (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)

After suffering their second loss in two nights to the Texas Rangers, the Toronto Blue Jays are now three games away from making the playoffs.
Meanwhile, the Chicago White Sox defeated the Detroit Tigers 3-1.
Yesterday's 6-2 loss in Arlington stings, and this win by the Rangers puts them in first place in the American League West this morning. It's now up to the Houston Astros to deal with the pressure of clinching a playoff spot. The other Texas team is just two games away from its goal.
With only seven regular-season games left to play, let's just say time is running out for John Schneider's squad. Does the team's 76-79 record perfectly reflect its performance so far? In my opinion, this record reveals a team that has been searching for its identity for much of the season and has had to deal with a number of injuries to key players. Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s disappointing season adds to the reasons that will be discussed in a few days.
Let's let the 2026 season run its course—the time for reckoning will come soon enough.
Yesterday, the Toronto offense once again lacked energy. Ever since setting foot on Texas soil, the Jays' hitters have been sluggish and unable to find a response to the Rangers' pitchers' offerings. In contrast, Skip Schumaker's men are playing with conviction and scoring early in the game, giving themselves every chance to win.
In the West, the Rangers have been playing much better baseball than the Astros lately, and seeing their roles reversed yesterday comes as no surprise to me. The Blue Jays arrived in Texas at the wrong time and with the wrong attitude. It looks like they're running on fumes.
The Jays' bats managed just six hits in this game. Alejandro Kirk and Davis Schneider drove in the team's runs. Schneider hit his fourth home run of the season, a solo shot off Rangers reliever Robert Garcia. Schneider was batting as a pinch hitter at the time.
José Soriano pitched five innings for his team and allowed six runs to the home team, five of which were earned. The Rangers scored all their runs on just five hits throughout the game. When it comes to capitalizing on opportunities, it doesn't get much better than that.
Due to the situation affecting his starting rotation, John Schneider has no choice but to turn to his bullpen for another “bullpen day” today, to close out this series against the Rangers. Spencer Miles will start for his team and face the always tough Jacob deGrom. Spencer Arrighetti will also see action.
Tomorrow, in Baltimore, Trey Yesavage will return to action against the Orioles. A long-awaited—but belated—return.
Everyone knew the race for the playoffs would be exciting in the American League, but Jays fans would certainly have preferred a better scenario than the one we're seeing right now. The final home stand against the Reds is likely to be largely meaningless, much to the chagrin of the team's fans.

20 Sep 2026, 13:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Arianna Grainey)
Pinch hitter Pavin Smith hit a two-run, walk-off homer with one out in the ninth and the Arizona Diamondbacks beat the New York Yankees 5-3 on Saturday in Phoenix on a night the franchise celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series victory over the Yankees.
Ildemaro Vargas walked to lead off the ninth off Michael Fulmer (0-1), reaching base after he appealed the 3-2 pitch that originally was called a strike. After a strikeout, Smith hit a 391-foot homer to right center for the D-backs' 46th comeback win of the season
Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells hit bases-empty homers for the Yankees, who had won four of five and eight of 10. Wells and Jose Caballero had two hits apiece.
Nolan Arenado had two hits and Jordan Lawlar added a two-run triple for the D-backs, who had lost three in a row and five of six.
The Yankees (89-65), who have clinched a playoff berth, fell five games behind Tampa Bay (94-60) in the American League East and remained 5 1/2 games ahead of Boston (84-71) for the top AL wild-card spot. The Yankees and Rays play a four-game series in Yankee Stadium beginning with a split doubleheader Tuesday.
White Sox 3, Tigers 1
Sean Burke hurled six quality innings and Miguel Vargas homered to help Chicago earn a victory over visiting Detroit.
Burke (10-7) allowed one run on five hits for Chicago, which remained a game behind American League Central-leading Cleveland. Sam Antonacci and Munetaka Murakami both drove in a run and Grant Taylor delivered a four-out save, his 10th overall this season.
Jackson Jobe (2-3) threw six innings of three-run, four-hit ball, striking out nine for Detroit, which remains barely alive in AL Central contention. The Tigers' wild-card elimination magic number is down to one. Kevin McGonigle drove in Detroit's lone run.
Mets 10, Phillies 3
Francisco Alvarez had two hits, including the go-ahead three-run homer in the fifth, as host New York routed skidding Philadelphia.
Carson Benge was 3-for-4 with a solo homer and two RBIs for the Mets. Brett Baty had two hits, including a run-scoring single, while Benge, Juan Soto and Bo Bichette each had RBI singles during a four-run eighth.
Alec Bohm had RBI singles in the fourth and fifth for the Phillies, who missed a chance to take over the top National League wild card, at least temporarily. The Cubs and Padres both won to remain tied atop the NL wild-card race.
Brewers 1, Orioles 0Robert Gasser pitched seven shutout innings as the first of three Milwaukee pitchers in a victory against host Baltimore.
It marked the second shutout for Milwaukee pitchers in an eight-game stretch, needing only four strikeouts for the latest accomplishment. The Brewers scored on Gary Sanchez's second-inning groundout to knock in Joey Ortiz, who tripled with one out.Baltimore has lost the first two games of the series following a three-game winning streak, further damaging its American League playoff hopes. Orioles starter Trevor Rogers (10-11) lasted eight innings, allowing one run and three hits.
Rangers 6, Blue Jays 2Texas won for the sixth time in its past seven games, defeating Toronto in Arlington, Texas.Rangers starting pitcher Cal Quantrill left the game after 1 1/3 innings with right lat tightness. Jordan Montgomery (1-0) replaced him and held Toronto hitless through 3 2/3 innings. Josh Jung gave Texas a 1-0 lead in the bottom of the first with a home run to right field.Jose Soriano (12-8) gave up six runs (five earned) on four hits and struck out eight in five-plus innings for the Blue Jays, who dropped to three games behind the Chicago White Sox for the final wild-card berth in the American League.
Rays 2, Red Sox 1
Richie Palacios produced a two-out, walk-off single in the ninth inning as Tampa Bay edged Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla., to even their final home series of the regular season.
Against Garrett Whitlock (7-2), Palacios looped a 1-2 sinker into right to score Junior Caminero as the Rays hit their third walk-off winner during their nine-game homestand. Jonathan Aranda homered while Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson posted two hits apiece.
Caleb Durbin stroked two doubles and scored for the Red Sox, who lost for the first time in three games. Starting pitcher Brayan Bello went a season-best eight innings and allowed one run on five hits with a career high-tying 11 strikeouts.
Guardians 12, Athletics 6
Angel Martinez homered from both sides of the plate and drove in four runs in host Cleveland's win over the Athletics which helped maintain its one-game lead in the American League Central.
Martinez was also 4-for-5 with a double and three runs scored and Chase DeLauter also homered for the Guardians, who won their fourth straight. Slade Cecconi (5-7) got the win in relief with two scoreless innings after Tanner Bibee lasted 4 2/3 innings and surrendered six runs on 12 hits.
Donovan Walton hit a home run and was 3-for-3 with four RBIs for the Athletics, who have lost five in a row. Athletics starter and loser Jacob Lopez (6-5) was blitzed for 10 runs and 10 hits in 2 2/3 innings.
Nationals 8, Cardinals 5 (11 innings)Jose Tena's two-run double keyed a four-run 11th inning and Washington beat the Cardinals in St. Louis.Jorbit Vivas had four hits and Daylen Lile homered for Washington, which has won six of seven. Riley Cornelio (3-2) pitched 1 2/3 innings for the win.At the top of the order, Jose Fermin and Ivan Herrera had three hits each for St. Louis, which has lost four straight.
Cubs 5, Reds 2
Michael Busch and Dansby Swanson hit solo home runs to lift visiting Chicago to a win over Cincinnati.
The win allowed the Cubs to pull a full game ahead of the Philadelphia Phillies for the top wild-card playoff spot in the National League. The Phillies lost 10-3 to the Mets earlier. The San Diego Padres also won to remain tied with the Cubs.
The teams will play the rubber game of the series Sunday. Cubs starter Matthew Boyd (9-5) gave up two hits and two runs (one earned) in five innings. Reds starter Nick Lodolo (3-6) gave up seven hits and three runs in seven innings.
Pirates 6, Royals 5
Brandon Lowe launched a go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth inning to power Pittsburgh to a victory over visiting Kansas City.
Ronny Simon and Jake Mangum each hit two-run homers, while Oneil Cruz, Rafael Flores Jr. and Lowe each had two hits for the Pirates. Right-hander Luke Weaver (3-1) threw a scoreless eighth with one strikeout, and left-hander Mason Montgomery earned his 15th save of the season after working around a walk with one strikeout in a scoreless ninth.
Nick Loftin had four hits, while Bobby Witt Jr. went 3-for-5 with two runs and extended his on-base streak to 17 games for the Royals. Carter Jensen hit a solo homer, while Jac Caglianone and Vinnie Pasquantino each had two hits for Kansas City.
Braves 6, Astros 3Ronald Acuna Jr. hit a grand slam, Grant Holmes produced a quality start and Atlanta lowered its magic number to one to clinch the National League East by defeating host Houston.The Braves secured this three-game interleague series and set the table to win the NL East for the seventh time in nine seasons with a victory in the series finale on Sunday. Holmes (10-5) allowed two runs on eight hits over six innings. Closer Raisel Iglesias notched his 34th save for Atlanta.The Astros dropped a game behind the Rangers in the AL West after Texas beat Toronto. Astros reliever AJ Blubaugh (5-3) loaded the bases and was replaced by Bryan Abreu, who gave up Acuna's homer in the seventh inning for a 5-2 Braves lead.Rockies 5, Mariners 3
Cole Carrigg delivered a go-ahead two-run single in a four-run seventh inning as Colorado edged Seattle in Denver.
Juan Mejia (4-6) pitched two scoreless innings and Brennan Bernardino got the final three outs for his second save for Colorado. Jake McCarthy and TJ Rumfield each produced an RBI.
Cal Raleigh and Randy Arozarena homered and Julio Rodriguez and Michael Arroyo had two hits each for Seattle, which is on the brink of elimination in the AL wild-card race.
Padres 6, Marlins 5 (10 innings)
Rookie Ethan Salas stroked an RBI single in the bottom of the 10th inning and San Diego edged visiting Miami.
Salas' hit scored Jake Cronenworth, who started the inning as the automatic runner at second base and advanced to third on a wild pitch by Josh Ekness (2-4). David Morgan (4-1) stranded runners at first and second in the top of the 10th to earn the win, San Diego's 12th in 13 games.
The Padres tied the Chicago Cubs for the top wild-card spot in the National League at 86-69. Miami forced extra innings when pinch hitter Griffin Conine pulled a 102 mph fastball from closer Mason Miller for a game-tying homer with one out in the ninth.
Dodgers 10, Giants 4
Mookie Betts tied a season high with four hits, Tommy Edman delivered a go-ahead two-run single and Los Angeles stayed within two games of the best record in the National League with a victory over visiting San Francisco.
Betts has 10 hits over his past three games, including seven in the past two while operating out of the leadoff spot in place of an injured Shohei Ohtani. Will Smith homered as the Dodgers won for the fifth time in six games and improved to 13-3 since Sept. 3. Tarik Skubal (11-7) gave up four runs on eight hits over five innings.
Victor Bericoto hit a home run among his two hits for the Giants while Yunior Marte (0-1) gave up six runs on eight hits over 4 2/3 innings in his fourth career appearance and second start.
Angels 6, Twins 5 (11 innings)Christian Moore singled in automatic runner Zach Neto with a bases-loaded comebacker off pitcher Taylor Rogers' leg with two outs in the bottom of the 11th inning as Los Angeles edged Minnesota in Anaheim, Calif.Moore drilled a first-pitch sweeper that caromed off the leg of Rogers (6-4) and back toward the third base line as Neto sprinted home. Tayler Saucedo (1-1) struck out two during a scoreless inning of relief for the Angels, who tied it at 5-5 in the bottom of the ninth on Vaughn Grissom's homer.Ryan Kreidler hit a home run, Victor Caratini went 2-for-5 with two RBIs, Walker Jenkins had two hits and a run and Josh Bell and Royce Lewis each had two hits for the Twins.

Palacios has RBI single in the 9th to Give the Rays a 2-1 Victory over the Red Sox
Richie Palacios dropped a fly ball into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, opened a five-game lead over the second-place New York Yankees in the AL East.
Prior to Palacios' single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong's passed ball moved Caminero to third.
The Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got Caleb Durbin's double and Jarren Duran's triple. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with bookend doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Up next
RHP Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.
