ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation.
The Red Sox couldn't close the deal in securing a postseason berth, succumbing to a Rays 2-1 walk-off win at Tropicana Field on Saturday. But an interesting development emerged along the way. Brayan Bello is suddenly a potential huge part of the postseason solution.
The almost out-of-nowhere conversation about Bello's importance was given an enormous boost by one of the pitcher's best outings of his career. Not only did Bello hold the Rays to just one run over eight innings, but he also struck out 11 and walked no one.
Why was this even more impressive than simply the end-of-day box score? Because Bello managed all those punchouts, along with 17 whiffs, against a Rays team that has struck out fewer times than any club in baseball. No starting pitcher had managed double-digit strikeouts against Tampa Bay, with Toronto's Dylan Cease coming the closest with nine.
Bello matches his career high with 11 strikeouts! pic.twitter.com/NA2a2pDcAy
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
The dominance was just what the doctor ordered for Bello and the Red Sox, even if starting a postseason game isn't in the righty's immediate future.
While there has been no announcement, it appears the Red Sox are lining up their wild-card rotation with Payton Tolle to pitch Game 1 against the Yankees, followed by Sonny Gray and then Ranger Suarez if Game 3 is needed in the best-of-three series. But that doesn't mean Bello can't have an impact on outcomes from late September into October.
Bello's fastball routinely sat at 97 mph, almost two mph above his season-average velocity. It was a fastball that got nine whiffs, with the Rays coming away with just four hard-hit balls all day.
"That was exceptional," Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. "By far and away, his best outing of the year, as good as I've seen him, so, I don't know what else to say, he was awesome. Really awesome."
Bello's appearance allowed for thoughts on what might be in store for his effectiveness out of the bullpen in high-leverage situations come Sept. 29. It has been well-documented what he can do as a reliever, posting a 1.98 ERA in 15 games out of the bullpen this season. But now we're not just talking about bulk roles or giving the Red Sox some length.
This version of Bello can absolutely be a late-inning, high-leverage weapon.
For instance, while we aren't sure of Aaron Judge's health heading into the postseason, if the Yankees' slugger does play, this might not be a bad reminder to put in your statistical back pocket: Judge is just 2-for-21 with eight strikeouts against Bello.
While some naysayers might point to the less-than-inspiring appearances Bello has turned in at Yankee Stadium as of late, including maybe his worst relief outing of the season at the end of August when he allowed four runs over 4 1/3 innings, or the 2 1/3-inning start in Game 2 of last season's wild card round. But before those two, the pitcher had been absolutely nails in the Bronx, totaling a 1.44 ERA in five starts.
Assuming their health is OK, the Red Sox will have Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock at the ready to help close out games. But with a week to go in the regular season, there is some uncertainty regarding the late-inning options. Saturday, Bello sure seemed like he was ready to help with that.
“For me, it's just showing the team that I'm ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.”

Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Richie Palacios dropped a blooper into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, lowered its magic number to clinch the AL East to five games. The second-place Yankees are in Arizona on Saturday night.
Prior to Palacios’ single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong’s passed ball moved Caminero to third.
Bidding to clinch a wild-card berth, the Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got a double from Caleb Durbin and a triple from Jarren Duran. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third before Duran’s triple, and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Boston could have clinched a playoff berth with a win combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros. Both of those teams were seven games behind the Red Sox with eight games remaining entering Saturday.
UP NEXT
Right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.

The Red Sox were one swing away from punching their ticket to October. Instead, they’ll have to wait at least one more day.
Richie Palacios dumped a walk-off single into right field off Garrett Whitlock in the bottom of the ninth inning Saturday, lifting the Rays to a 2-1 win over the Red Sox at Tropicana Field and preventing Boston from clinching a postseason berth.
The Rays pieced together three singles against Whitlock in the ninth after the teams entered the inning tied at 1. Boston had opportunities to push across the go-ahead run in the later innings but couldn’t capitalize, wasting an outstanding performance from Brayan Bello.
Bello turned in arguably his most impressive start of the season, allowing just one run on five hits over eight innings while striking out 11 to match his career high.
“That was exceptional,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters following the game. “By far and away his best outing of the year. As good as I’ve seen him. So, I don’t know what else to say. He was awesome, really awesome.”
It marked the second consecutive scoreless start for Bello, but Saturday’s outing was far more dominant than his previous one. Against the Angels at Fenway Park, Bello navigated almost constant traffic, allowing four hits and two walks while needing 103 pitches to complete five innings.
Bello needed just 55 pitches to complete his first five innings and kept the Rays off balance throughout the afternoon. He allowed only one run, a Jonathan Aranda’s solo homer leading off the fourth, and gave the Red Sox exactly what they needed with two of their most important late-inning relievers unavailable.
“I just felt confident attacking the zone,” Bello told reporters via team translator.
Bello isn’t expected to start in the Wild Card Series, but his recent performances have provided a reminder of the value he could offer in October. After an uneven season that eventually resulted in a move to the bullpen, he has reestablished himself as someone Tracy can trust in a meaningful spot.
Aranda’s homer was notable for another reason. It was the first home run Bello had allowed since July 12, the final game before the All-Star break, snapping a homerless stretch of roughly 42 innings. Much of that work came in relief, often following an opener, but going more than two months without surrendering a homer remains an impressive run.
“For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for this kind of games,” Bello added.
For the second straight game, Roman Anthony provided Boston with some early offense.
After leading off Friday’s victory with a 438-foot homer, Anthony delivered again in the third inning Saturday. Caleb Durbin opened the inning with a double before Anthony sliced an RBI double into left-center to give Boston a 1-0 lead.
The productive at-bats are an encouraging development for Anthony after his recent slump. With the postseason just over a week away, the rookie is beginning to show signs of heating up at the right time.
Durbin may be coming out of a slump of his own.
After collecting two hits in Friday’s series opener, Durbin added two more Saturday, both sharply hit doubles. His offensive turnaround earlier this season coincided with Boston’s surge up the standings, and another hot stretch would add length to the lineup and provide another productive right-handed bat heading into October.

As the Red Sox fell to the Rays 2-1 at Tropicana Field on Saturday evening, wasting an excellent start by homegrown right-hander Brayan Bello, a similar scenario played out between the division rivals’ Triple-A affiliates.
The WooSox lost their penultimate game of the season to the Durham Bulls 4-3 in 10 innings, despite 3 1/3 innings of solid relief work from fellow homegrown Red Sox righty Tanner Houck, who is nearing a return from Tommy John surgery in August 2025.
Houck faced 12 batters, and allowed one earned run and one unearned, on two hits, struck out two and did not issue a walk.
Bulls catcher Tatem Levins scored both runs, but his only true damage off Houck was a one-out 431-foot solo homer in the seventh. Houck’s unearned run came after Sam McWilliams relieved him with one out in the 10th; McWilliams gave up an RBI single to Homer Bush Jr., and Levins scored as the automatic runner.
The Red Sox have not determined next steps for Houck, but they are planning to use him in a relief role. He could be activated during their final homestand, which begins Tuesday versus the Cleveland Guardians.
Houck is the longest-tenured Red Sox major leaguer in the organization, having debuted Sept. 15, 2020. He owns a career 3.97 ERA over six big-league seasons, a mark inflated by his 8.04 ERA in nine starts before the season-ending surgery last year.

Rays continue walk-off winning ways against Red Sox
(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
Richie Palacios produced a two-out, walk-off single in the ninth inning as the Tampa Bay Rays edged the Boston Red Sox 2-1 on Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla., to even their final home series of the regular season.
Against Garrett Whitlock (7-2), Palacios looped a 1-2 sinker into shallow right to score Junior Caminero as the Rays (94-60) hit their third walk-off winner during the nine-game homestand.
Jonathan Aranda homered while Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson posted two hits apiece as Tampa Bay improved to 7-1 on the homestand.
Bidding for a fifth consecutive win over five starts, Freddy Peralta received no decision after yielding just one run on four hits over 5 2/3 innings that took 97 pitches. He struck out six and walked two.
Caleb Durbin stroked two doubles and scored for the Red Sox (84-71), who lost for the first time in three games.
Starting pitcher Brayan Bello went a season-best eight innings and allowed one run on five hits with a career high-tying 11 strikeouts.
The Rays got an out with the infield drawn in and appeared to escape trouble in the third. Then Roman Anthony, who homered and had three RBIs in Friday's 4-2 win in the opener, remained hot and made it 1-0 with a two-out double that scored Durbin.
Cedric Mullins laid down a bunt single and reached second on Durbin's throwing error to open the third, but he was picked off and caught trying to steal third on Jorge Mateo's failed sacrifice bunt.
In the fourth, Aranda tied it 1-all when he rocked his 22nd homer to left field as he took Bello's 97 m.p.h. four-seam fastball the opposite way.
With Bello still in the game in the seventh, Hicks led off with a single and Simpson dropped one into right with no outs. Following a groundout and a fielder's choice, Bello ended the threat by whiffing Mullins on a foul tip.
Durbin lined his second double with one out in the ninth, but Hicks tossed him out trying to steal third. Jarren Duran followed with his fifth triple, but Isiah Kiner-Falefa grounded out to deep third to end the inning off Bryan Baker (4-2).
--Field Level Media

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Brayan Bello, a pitcher who lost his spot in the rotation earlier in this season, did his best to pitch the Red Sox into the postseason on Saturday afternoon, allowing one run over eight innings against the Rays.
But it was not enough.
The Rays walked-off the Sox in the ninth inning with a 2-1 victory before a crowd of 27,402 at Tropicana Field as Richie Palacios had a two-out run-scoring single.
Bello gave up only five hits and struck out 11 — matching his career high — without a walk.
The loss left the Red Sox with a magic number of two.
In a tense game between two teams who could well meet in October, the Sox missed numerous chances to score. They were for 1 for 11 with runners in scoring position and left eight runners on base.
They left a runner on second in the eighth inning and another on third in the ninth.
Facing Garrett Whitlock (7-2) in the ninth inning, Junior Caminero led off with a single — after his potentially playable foul popup struck a catwalk and was ruled a dead ball.
Chandler Simpson singled with one out. A passed ball by Connor Wong moved the runners up. Palacios then won the game with a soft single to shallow right field.
The early innings were a duel between Bello and Rays starter Freddy Peralta.
Peralta retired the first six Red Sox in order, four by swinging strikeout. Caleb Durbin led off the third inning with a double to left field. Jarren Duran sacrificed Durbin to third before Roman Anthony delivered an RBI double to center field.
The Rays tied the game when Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom of the fourth inning with a home run to left field when Bello left a first-pitch fastball over the plate.
Peralta gave up four hits and walked two over 5⅔ innings and 97 pitches but allowed only the one run. The Sox were 1 for 7 with runners in scoring position against him.
Bello had only 68 pitches through six innings. Liam Hicks and Simpson singled on his first two pitches of the seventh inning. With Jonny DeLuca running for Hicks, the runners moved up when Victor Mesa Jr. grounded to second.
With the infield in, Palacios grounded to shortstop. Trevor Story snapped the ball up and fired to the plate to get DeLuca. Bello then struck out Cedric Mullins with a 96.8-mile-per-hour fastball.

Someone only tuning into their first Red Sox game of the season Saturday might not understand the significance of Brayan Bello’s dominant performance against the hosting Tampa Bay Rays.
Particularly as it will be forever marred by a Rays’ 2-1 walk-off victory that keeps Boston’s postseason ticket dangling out of reach for at least another night.
But before that frustrating ending, there was Bello’s hard-earned triumph. It has been a tumultuous year for the homegrown right-hander, who lost his spot in the Red Sox starting rotation at the beginning of May, and pitched his way into a Triple-A demotion the first week of June. Bello dominated in a bulk-relief role from his mid-July recall through early September before the Red Sox gave him another chance to start.
Making his second start of the month on Saturday, Bello turned in not only his best game of the season, but one of the best of his five-year career. He owned his team’s first-place division rivals for eight innings of one-run ball. He yielded just five hits, issued no walks and matched his career-high 11 strikeouts.
“That was exceptional,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “By far and away his best outing of the year. As good as I’ve seen him. So, I don’t know what else to say. He was awesome, really awesome.”
Bello’s reward was a no-decision, as the Red Sox lineup went 1 for 11 with runners in scoring position, then lost on Rays second baseman Richie Palacios’ walk-off RBI single in the bottom of the ninth.
Palacios’ game-winning hit came moments after a base-running gamble by Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin that proved calamitous. A glimmer of hope flared when Durbin collected his second double of the day, off Bryan Baker with one out in the top of the ninth. But he was then caught trying to steal third, which proved costly almost instantaneously when Jarren Duran tripled on the very next pitch. Isiah Kiner-Falefa’s inning-ending groundout sent the tie game to the bottom of the ninth.
“I’m OK with it,” Tracy said of Durbin’s attempt to steal. “It’s one-to-one game the whole way, and close play.”
“Hindsight is 20/20,” Tracy continued. “It’s easy in baseball. He gets thrown out, and then Duran has a triple. But you don’t have the privilege of hindsight. So (Durbin) was working hard out there, seeing if he can get the bag, and they got him.”
“I thought I had a window, and probably wasn’t a big enough window,” Durbin told reporters. “I those situations, too, you want to be sure about it. So obviously on me. Not really any excuse other than I gotta be more sure.”
Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox an early lead for the second straight game, doubling off Rays starter Freddy Peralta with two outs in the third. Anthony’s third RBI base hit of the series scored Durbin, who led off the frame with his first double.
But that was all the Red Sox wrote. The home team peppered the middle innings with costly mistakes, but the visitors never took advantage.
Rays centerfielder Cedric Mullins reached safely on a bunt single and advanced to second on a throwing error by Durbin to begin the bottom of the third, but Boston’s third baseman immediately atoned for the miscue by completing a caught-stealing relay with catcher Adley Rutschman and shortstop Trevor Story.
Tampa Bay ran out of ABS challenges by the fourth inning. Shortstop Jorge Mateo burned one on a called Strike 3 from Bello (1.2” Edge Distance) for the second out of the bottom of the third. Peralta lost his team’s remaining bid trying to overturn a Ball 4 with a 2.8” Edge Distance, which put right-fielder Wilyer Abreu on with one out in the fourth.
The worm turned in the bottom of the fourth. Boston’s squandering of a one-out opportunity with Abreu and Nick Sogard (single) on first and second in the top of the inning proved costly immediately when Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom with a first-pitch, game-tying home run.
An undeterred Bello held fast to the knot inning after inning, and looked effortless doing so. Whereas Peralta exited after 5 2/3 innings that required 97 pitches (59 for strikes), Bello needed 55 pitches to complete the first five frames, and his count sat at 68 at the end of the sixth.
When the Rays finally threatened in the bottom of the seventh, the Sox starter was the picture of poise. Unruffled by the back-to-back singles by Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson, Bello retired the next three men in order. The game became his longest of the season as a starter or reliever when he recorded the first out of the seventh, and when he returned to the dugout after finishing the eighth inning, it marked his deepest outing since his complete game on July 8, 2025.
With closer Aroldis Chapman still unavailable due to lat tightness, it fell to righty Garrett Whitlock to pitch the game to extra innings. Whitlock was one strike away from stranding slugger Junior Caminero and Simpson when Palacios sent his 1-2 sinker to right field, where it plunked down in front of Abreu.
The loss means Sunday is the earliest the Red Sox can punch their ticket to October. The current playoff picture has the Red Sox and Yankees meeting in a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium. If Boston gets beyond that, they could see Tampa Bay again.
Saturday’s intensity felt like a preview to the Red Sox. Durbin hopes they can turn the experience into an advantage.
“That was a hell of a baseball game,” Tracy said. “I don’t have really anything negative to say about that game, other than it was really well-played on both sides by both teams. Big moments, and people rose the occasion. It was just a heck of a baseball game, and they were able to beat us.”
“Even yesterday and tomorrow, like they got a little bit of a playoff feel,” Durbin said. “I feel like last year (with the Milwaukee Brewers), first couple playoff games … adrenaline’s way higher. So to get that feel before playoffs even start is super important, because it usually takes a couple games to really settle in. So if we could settle in by Game 1 or 2, that’ll be big for us.”

The Boston Red Sox could not have asked much more from Brayan Bello on Saturday. Unfortunately for Boston, nearly everything around him went wrong at the worst possible moments.
Bello delivered eight outstanding innings, but the Red Sox squandered several scoring opportunities before the Tampa Bay Rays walked off with a 2-1 victory at Tropicana Field. Richie Palacios ended the game with a two-out single off Garrett Whitlock, bringing Junior Caminero home from third base. The loss dropped Boston to 84-71 and evened the three-game series at one victory apiece.
Here are four takeaways from Saturday’s game:
Bello Brilliant In Tough-Luck Start
Bello did everything necessary to earn a victory. The right-hander allowed only one earned run on five hits over eight innings. He did not issue a walk, struck out 11 and threw 65 of his 93 pitches for strikes.
FINAL: Rays 2, #RedSox 1
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
Bello retired the first three batters he faced and struck out seven through his first five innings. Tampa Bay’s only run against him came when Jonathan Aranda opened the fourth inning with a 361-foot home run.
The Rays threatened again in the seventh after singles from Lathan Hicks and Chandler Simpson placed two runners aboard with nobody out. Bello escaped without allowing a run, getting Víctor Mesa Jr. on a groundout, Palacios on a fielder’s choice at the plate and Cedric Mullins on a strikeout.
Bello finished the eighth by retiring Tampa Bay in order. He set down 17 of the final 20 hitters he faced and ended the afternoon with a season-high 11 strikeouts.
Boston Offense Wastes Its Chances
The Red Sox collected eight hits but finished only 1-for-11 with runners in scoring position and stranded eight runners. Boston scored its only run in the third inning. Caleb Durbin opened the frame with a double, advanced to third on Jarren Duran’s sacrifice bunt and scored when Roman Anthony doubled to center field.
That was all the Red Sox produced against Freddy Peralta and four Tampa Bay relievers.
Boston placed two runners aboard in both the fourth and sixth innings without scoring. Adley Rutschman doubled with one out in the eighth, but Wilyer Abreu struck out and Nick Sogard lined out to end the threat.
The most frustrating missed opportunity arrived in the ninth.
Durbin doubled with one out but was caught trying to steal third. Duran then tripled to center field, a hit that almost certainly would have scored Durbin had he remained at second. Isiah Kiner-Falefa grounded out to strand Duran and keep the game tied.
Ninth Inning Unravels On Whitlock
Whitlock entered for the bottom of the ninth after Bello’s terrific afternoon and immediately surrendered a single to Caminero. Whitlock retired Jonny DeLuca before Simpson added another single. A passed ball charged to Connor Wong moved both runners into scoring position, although Whitlock responded by striking out Mesa for the second out.
He could not escape the inning.
Palacios lined a 2-2 sinker into right field, allowing Caminero to score the winning run. The run was unearned because of Wong’s passed ball, but Whitlock took the loss after surrendering three hits in two-thirds of an inning.
MORE: How the Red Sox Can Clinch a Playoff Spot on Saturday
Series Finale Takes On Added Importance
Boston entered Saturday with a chance to take another significant step toward securing its postseason spot after winning Friday’s series opener. Instead, the Red Sox will need to regroup quickly following one of their most frustrating losses of the season.
The defeat dropped Boston to 84-71 and left the Red Sox 10 1/2 games behind the first-place Rays in the American League East. More importantly, it prevented Boston from building additional momentum in the wild-card race.
The Red Sox and Rays will decide the series Sunday at Tropicana Field. First pitch is scheduled for 3:10 p.m. ET.

Sonny Gray? Ranger Suarez? Payton Tolle? Who should get the ball in game one in the Bronx for the Red Sox?
To manage the starting rotation workload and line up the rotation for the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox are turning to Brayan Bello to start Saturday's game against the Tampa Bay Rays. Whether the Red Sox go with Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, or Payton Tolle, the team will feel very good about its chances of winning. However, if the team gets swept, it risks leaving an incredible arm on the bench.
Let's take a look at the argument for each of the trio to get the ball in game one:
Gray
The 36-year-old veteran has inarguably been the Red Sox' best starter in 2026. After entering the season with questions about how effective he could be late in his career, Gray has passed every test with flying colors. In 28 starts, Gray has posted a 2.82 ERA, the eighth-lowest mark in the league, while the Red Sox have gone 20-8 on his start days.
Most importantly, even when he doesn't have his best stuff, he has done well to limit damage; of his 28 starts, he has allowed more than three runs on four occasions. In two starts against the New York Yankees in 2026, Gray has allowed only three earned runs on nine hits, while striking out 12 and walking only four. In his career, Gray has a solid record of playoff success, posting a 3.26 ERA in 30.1 innings.
However, when it comes to elite strikeout stuff that can completely shut down a lineup, Gray lacks that, posting a rather pedestrian strikeouts per nine innings of 8.06, which ranks 30th out of 48 qualified starters.
Still though, Gray appears to be the most obvious choice to get the start in game one.
Suarez
The Red Sox' most difficult decision with their postseason rotation may be the one they have to make with Suarez. The 30-year-old All-Star signed a five-year, $130-million deal with the Red Sox in the offseason, in part because he posted an impressive 1.48 ERA over 42.2 innings with the Philadelphia Phillies.
However, of the trio in consideration, Suarez has been the shakiest since the All-Star break, posting a 3.46 ERA in his last 10 starts. However, the three-time All-Star has been better lately, allowing only two earned runs in 19.2 innings across three starts. Suarez has struggled against the Yankees in three starts in 2026, allowing 11 runs on 20 hits for a 6.06 ERA.
Still, it seems unlikely the team would risk leaving its $130 million investment on the sidelines for a playoff series.
Tolle
The 23-year-old rookie has been Boston's best starter since the All-Star break. In his last 10 starts, Tolle has posted a 2.90 ERA while striking out 12.05 batters per nine innings, the fifth-highest mark among 93 pitchers with at least 50 innings pitched.
Tolle has also performed incredibly well against the Yankees, allowing only one earned run on four hits while striking out 18 and walking only four. Tolle is also the only pitcher on the Boston staff with the electric stuff that could match New York ace Cam Schlittler in shutting down the lineup.
While it certainly may seem risky to some to give a 23-year-old rookie the ball in game one in Yankee Stadium, how can you risk not throwing him at all?
Up next for the Sox
With their magic number down to two, the Red Sox will look to win a series against the likely American League East champion Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday afternoon. Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.74 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) will start for Tampa. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 4:10 p.m. ET.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.
Boston regional outlet MassLive also highlighted the performances of Gamboa and Alls on the 17th, saying, "He seized an unexpected opportunity this year, expanded his standing, and his entry into the postseason roster race—which would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago—is worthy of high praise," introducing that Gamboa has performed well enough to be included on the postseason roster.
Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.
He had an especially strong performance, including being named player of the month for June, but fatigue accumulated late in the season and elbow pain caused him to miss several turns in the rotation, preventing a smooth finish. His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.
Although Gamboa failed to re-sign with Lotte, he said of going to Lotte, "It was a good opportunity to show myself elsewhere. I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.

The Boston Red Sox open up a three-game series against AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, September 18, at Tropicana Field.
Ranger Suarez will get the ball for Boston tonight. After that, the pitching plans are unclear. The Red Sox have listed TBDs for their starting pitcher spot on Saturday and Sunday, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. Payton Tolle and Patrick Sandoval were lined up to start this weekend, but that is now in doubt.
Probable pitchers for Red Sox-Rays this weekend…
* Friday: Ranger Suarez vs. Ian Seymour* Saturday: TBD vs. Freddy Peralta* Sunday: TBD vs. Griffin Jax
Saturday would be Payton Tolle's day, if the Red Sox stay on turn. We'll see how they handle it.
— Tim Healey (@timbhealey) September 17, 2026
Tolle has already zoomed past his previous career high in innings as a pro. The lefty tossed 108 frames between the minors and majors in 2025. Tolle has thrown 158 innings across both levels this season.
Boston Red Sox May Skip Payton Tolle Against the Tampa Bay Rays
Tolle has been a fixture in Boston's rotation for much of the season. He's posted a 3.03 ERA across 25 starts with the big-league club. The young lefty opened the season in the minors, but was promoted to the majors in April. Tolle has solidified a pitching staff that has dealt with injuries and underperformance at times in 2026.
While he won't win AL Rookie of the Year, Tolle has put together a solid case. He's right up there with Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick as the top rookie starter in the American League. Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox are the betting favorites, but Tolle and Messick will receive some down-ballot votes.
Tolle struggled to a 6.06 ERA in his first taste of the big leagues last year. He missed bats at a decent 25.7% clip, but notched a 10.8% walk rate. The lefty has improved in both departments this season. Tolle pushed his strikeout rate to 28.9% and trimmed his walk rate to 6.6% in his first full campaign as a major league starter.
Red Sox Lining Up Postseason Rotation
Moving Tolle's next start could be an effort to align the playoff rotation. The pitching staff will likely be headlined by Sonny Gray, but the second and third slots are up for grabs. Suarez has a solid case to pitch the second game of the Wild Card round. The gig could also go to Tolle.
Sandoval and Jake Bennett are likely looking at long relief roles in the first round of the playoffs. Both have had decent stretches this season, but faded recently. Bennett has permitted a dozen runs in three September starts. Sandoval has a 7.82 ERA this month.
Brayan Bello is the question mark among the unit. He's struggled as a starter and been tremendous out of the bullpen. Bello could operate in tandem with one of Boston's many left-handed starters.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Originally viewed as one of the favorites to start the season in the Opening Day rotation, Red Sox right-hander Johan Oviedo wound up making just one appearance out of the bullpen before going on the shelf with a right elbow strain.
Now after missing nearly the entire season, Oviedo may finally be nearing a return.
Oviedo began a rehab assignment at Triple-A Worcester on Thursday, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in his first game action since late March.
The 28-year-old threw 30 pitches, 20 for strikes, while allowing one run on two hits and a walk while striking out four. Oviedo allowed an RBI double with one out in the top of the second before striking out the final three batters he faced.
More encouragingly, Oviedo’s fastball averaged 95.9 mph and topped out at 98.5, a sizable jump from the 92-93 he averaged earlier in the season.
Originally acquired last winter from the Pittsburgh Pirates as part of the Jhostynxon Garcia trade, Oviedo was initially expected to provide rotation depth as a possible high-ceiling power arm. Oviedo had previously missed extensive time due to Tommy John surgery, but finished his last season in Pittsburgh strong with a 3.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts over nine starts down the stretch.
The righty entered spring as one of the favorites for the No. 5 rotation spot, but after some promising early starts began showing signs of wear. The last rotation spot wound up going to Connelly Early, with Oviedo making the team as a reliever, and he made one appearance against the Houston Astros on March 30, allowing four runs over 3 2/3 innings.
Oviedo has been on the injured list ever since, but now he could be a dark horse candidate for the Red Sox playoff roster along with Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet, who are also working their way back from extended injury absences.
Upcoming starters
Ranger Suarez will start Friday’s series opener against the Tampa Bay Rays, but the Red Sox’s other starters remain to be determined. Payton Tolle would normally be in line to start Saturday but Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas on Thursday that the club is still deciding how it wants to handle the weekend.
Brayan Bello, who was limited to 19 pitches over 1 2/3 innings on Tuesday, would presumably be a candidate to start one of this weekend’s games.

The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though.
It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing.
"The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason," Cotillo wrote. "It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox haven't officially clinched a postseason spot, but all signs point toward a Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium.
Pitching depth was a problem for the Red Sox in last year's playoff meeting with the Yankees. Their ace Garrett Crochet propelled them to victory in Game 1, but Brayan Bello and an inexperienced Connelly Early couldn't get the job done in Games 2 and 3.
This time, Boston's pitching will be a strength. Veteran right-hander Sonny Gray, rookie southpaw Payton Tolle, and veteran lefty Ranger Suarez can go toe-to-toe with most clubs' 1-through-3. The question is, what's the optimal order to put them in for the three-game Wild Card Series?
It's a good problem to have, and there's really no wrong answer. That said, here's our ideal Wild Card Series rotation for Boston as it looks to avenge last year's crushing defeat:
Justin Leger
Game 1: Sonny Gray
Gray isn't the "sexy" pick. That would be the mustached man I have starting Game 2.
But in what's sure to be an electrifying environment at Yankee Stadium, I want a dependable veteran on the mound to begin the series. I want Mr. Consistency.
All season long, Gray has fit that description.
Gray has a 17-5 record (tied for MLB lead in wins) with a 2.76 ERA through 27 starts. Since Crochet went down with an early-season injury, the 36-year-old has stepped up as the Red Sox' de facto ace with 18 quality starts (tied for seventh in MLB).
Unlike Tolle, Gray has plenty of experience pitching at Yankee Stadium. He's had his fair share of rough starts there throughout his 14-year career, especially during his brief stint with New York, but he was solid there earlier this season with three earned runs across 6.1 innings pitched in a 5-3 victory. In his other start against the Yankees at Fenway Park, he took a no-hitter into the eighth inning.
It'll be an uphill battle for the Red Sox regardless of who's on the mound, because Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler will be poised to shut down Boston's bats yet again. Still, Gray can be counted on to give the Sox a chance to win, and if they lose, they'll have great options to lean on in Games 2 and 3.
Game 2: Payton Tolle
If Tolle is named the Red Sox' Game 1 starter, I won't complain. I'd be slightly concerned that his 0.1 IP in last year's Wild Card Series marks his only experience pitching at Yankee Stadium, but that isn't worth panicking about. He seems built for the bright lights.
Tolle looked sharp in both of his starts against the Yankees at Fenway this season. During his first outing in April, the 23-year-old allowed just one run on three hits across six innings. In his second start against them in June, he carried a perfect game into the sixth inning, finishing with no runs and just one hit allowed over seven innings pitched.
Those were two of many outings this season in which Tolle has looked like an ace. He'll have to perform like one throughout Boston's postseason run, and if he gets the ball in Game 2, he might be counted on to keep Boston's season alive.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
If it comes down to a do-or-die Game 3, I feel great about Ranger Suarez taking the mound. The 31-year-old veteran has the postseason pedigree with an impressive 1.48 ERA in 11 career appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
Suarez endured a second-half slump but has looked more like himself in his last two outings. After tossing seven shutout innings against the Baltimore Orioles on Sept. 4, he allowed just one run across seven innings while striking out eight Kansas City Royals hitters on Saturday. This is the version of Suarez the Red Sox expected to get when they signed him to a five-year, $130 million contract in the offseason.
If Suarez struggles, the Red Sox will have the luxury of an elite bullpen to lean on. Brayan Bello has been an excellent bulk option since reverting to a relief role. Jake Bennett could be a legitimate weapon out of the 'pen as well, along with Crochet if he returns in time from his injury.
Mitchael Hurley
Game 1: Payton Tolle
I'm not opposed to statistics influencing baseball decisions. I rely on statistics more than I should.
But in this case, I don't think they matter. If you've watched the Red Sox this year, it could not be more clear that Payton Tolle is very much the heart and soul of this team. And the idea of sending him out onto the mound at Yankee Stadium with the whole baseball world watching just feels like the obvious choice.
If the Red Sox are going to win a series like this one, they're going to need to be the team with more energy. Nobody would bring more juice to the mound than Tolle. If he can step onto the field on a rainy Sunday four hours after first pitch was scheduled and instantly deliver an immaculate inning in the first, it's frightening to think what type of energy he can bring to a Game 1 start.
The Yankees have struggled against him this year, but even if they hadn't, I've gotta send Tolle to the mound for Game 1.
Game 2: Sonny Gray
In another year, in another circumstance, the 36-year-old Sonny Gray would be in line to win his first career Cy Young Award.
Of course, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees' presumed Game 1 starter, has wrecked any and all Cy Young debate with his sterling season in New York. Still, Gray is having one of the best seasons of his 14-year career, and he has to pitch in this series.
He did allow a pair of homers in his lone start at Yankee Stadium this season, and he's given up 22 homers in 23 appearances there in his career. With the short porch looming and the crowd always looking to erupt, that would be my concern.
But Gray's been great all year, he's been great down the stretch, and the Red Sox will ensure that he's properly rested for this one.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
Would it look bad if the Red Sox potentially lost the series in two games and never sent Ranger Suarez and his 1.48 postseason ERA to the mound? It sure would.
But given the years that Tolle and Gray have had, I think the Red Sox could live with it.
There is some concern that he got rocked in the Bronx on Aug. 30 (six earned runs in 5.1 innings), but he also allowed one run in six innings in his first start at Yankee Stadium earlier in the season.
Considering the Red Sox had to send rookie Connelly Early out there in Game 3 a year ago to make his fifth career start, the team is clearly in a much better position if another Game 3 awaits them in the Bronx.

ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to securing a postseason berth after Toronto was routed by Detroit, reducing Boston’s magic number to five.
Any potential celebration will have to wait until after the Red Sox leave Texas. Even if Boston wins the final two games of the series, Toronto is off Thursday and would remain mathematically alive entering Friday.
Sandoval’s night began when he struck out the first four Rangers he faced before everything unraveled in a second inning that seemed as though it might never end.
With two outs, Brandon Nimmo and Ezequiel Duran delivered hard-hit singles at 106.3 mph and 105.3 mph, respectively. Elias Díaz followed by pulling a two-run double into left field to give Texas a 2-0 lead.
Sandoval never recovered walking former Sox catcher Danny Jansen and Justin Foscue before Corey Seager dropped a bloop single into shallow left, just beyond the reach of Trevor Story, allowing two more runs to score. By the time Sandoval finally escaped, he had thrown 44 pitches in the inning and Boston trailed 4-0.
Sandoval lasted just 2 2/3 innings and saw his ERA climb to 4.99.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
The left-hander’s return from injury provided Boston with some needed innings after he was activated July 9, and he delivered several quality outings along the way. But with the postseason approaching, his place on the October roster has become increasingly uncertain.
Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett are ahead of him in the rotation picture, while Brayan Bello has found success in a bulk role. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are also attempting to return before the postseason.
Patrick Sandoval strikes out the side in the 1st.
Justin Foscue made him throw 9 pitches to start the game. Needed 19 total to finish the inning. pic.twitter.com/qpUpDLA5Rc
Sandoval will have time to try and clean things up, but it’s looking as if the Red Sox are better suited with the lefty as a spectator when they inevitably travel to the Bronx.
Boston’s offense quickly cut the deficit in half against Jacob deGrom.
Nick Sogard jumped on a pitch in the third and sent it down the right-field line for a two-run homer, pulling the Red Sox within 4-2.
Sogard didn’t hit his first major league homer until his 322nd plate appearance Aug. 19. He has now hit five in his last 99 plate appearances, all coming over a 24-game span.
The versatile infielder contributed in other ways, too. Sogard perfectly executed a sacrifice bunt in the fifth to move two runners into scoring position and later made an athletic play to complete a 1-4-3 double play.
But the Red Sox couldn’t capitalize on their opportunities against deGrom. The Texas right-hander held Boston to three hits and struck out eight over five innings while maintaining a fastball around 97 mph.
